channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Weight-loss surgery produces lasting diabetes remission, long-term study finds
item.description: People with type 2 diabetes were much more likely to achieve remission after weight-loss surgery than after intensive medical and lifestyle management, according to a long-term study. Researchers also identified patient characteristics linked to remission and to the likelihood of diabetes returning.

item.title: Are you dressed yet? How parents can build child‑friendly routines that kids can follow
item.description: "Please go brush your teeth, get dressed and brush your hair." These are familiar morning requests that parents make to preschool and school-age children.

item.title: Added antibody step improves the reliability of Alzheimer's blood tests
item.description: Researchers at University Medicine Halle have developed a new method that could improve the reliability of blood tests for Alzheimer's disease. Current commercial tests often rely on the protein biomarker p-tau217, whose levels can rise in the early stages of the disease. However, the biomarker levels can also be elevated in other conditions, potentially leading to false-positive results. In a study involving 315 participants, the research team demonstrated improved accuracy in distinguishing Alzheimer's disease from other conditions. Their findings have been published in Nature Communications.

item.title: Long COVID linked to greater risk of high blood pressure
item.description: Long COVID is often associated with symptoms such as persistent fatigue, shortness of breath and brain fog. But evidence increasingly shows that long COVID may have a broad effect on the cardiovascular system, as well.

item.title: Location of rare cancer impacts survival, study suggests
item.description: A rare, aggressive cancer, commonly found in the uterus, limbs and abdomen, behaves differently depending on where it is found in the body, according to new research.

item.title: Viagra's cousin could help muscle cells stay primed for regeneration
item.description: Tadalafil is a prescription drug closely related to Viagra. It is used to treat erectile dysfunction (ED) and the urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate. Both competitive and recreational athletes sometimes use it too, to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a condition that can limit how well the body tolerates exercise.

item.title: Tired, irritable and craving carbs? Why darker days affect our bodies and brains
item.description: When the clocks go back in October, millions of Britons welcome an extra hour in bed. But by the evening, with darkness arriving before many people finish work, that small luxury may seem a distant memory.

item.title: One violin lesson changes brain wave patterns as beginners learn to play
item.description: A new study using wearable brain imaging has shown what happens in the human brain when someone learns to play a musical instrument. The results revealed the patterns of brain activity that enable us to play an instrument, in this case a violin, and how having just a single lesson significantly changes those patterns of activity.

item.title: Watching others face danger may shape how we learn, rat experiments suggest
item.description: Much of what we know about the world comes from experiences we have never had ourselves. A child observes how a parent reacts to a situation, which influences their own future actions. Someone becomes more cautious after seeing another person in danger.

item.title: New treatment approach shows promise in reducing prostate cancer spread
item.description: Adding darolutamide to standard treatment for aggressive prostate cancer reduced the risk of the disease spreading in an international phase 3 trial.

item.title: Fructose slows liver tumors in mice when key sugar-processing gene is missing, may lead to new treatments
item.description: Fructose is an important nutrient that, despite having a chemical structure very similar to that of glucose, is metabolized very differently in the body. Research into fructose metabolism and its regulation of metabolism in the human body has in recent years become a frontier topic in the life sciences and medicine. A new study led by researchers at City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) has found that in the specific metabolic context of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), dietary fructose does not fuel tumor growth. Instead, it can suppress it, revealing a previously unknown anticancer mechanism.

item.title: Previously unrecognized immune cells may drive harmful blood vessel growth in blinding eye diseases
item.description: A Northwestern Medicine study has identified a previously unrecognized population of immune cells that appears to fuel harmful blood vessel growth in multiple blinding eye diseases, according to the study published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The discovery could open the door to new treatments for patients who don't respond to existing therapies, said the study's senior author Jeremy Lavine, M.D., Ph.D., assistant professor of ophthalmology.

item.title: Biomarkers identified for cytokine release syndrome risk after CAR T-cell therapy
item.description: For patients with autoimmune disease, higher baseline B-cell counts and systemic inflammation are associated with development of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) after chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, according to a study published in the November issue of The Lancet Rheumatology.

item.title: Immunotherapy combo extends survival for patients with aggressive small cell lung cancer, based on trial results
item.description: In patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC), tarlatamab, a bispecific T-cell engager, plus durvalumab as first-line maintenance therapy extended median overall survival by more than eight months, more than tripled progression-free survival and reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to durvalumab alone, according to results of the phase 3 open-label, multicenter, randomized DeLLphi-305 study.

item.title: Florida dengue cases nearly double a month after emergency declared
item.description: Dengue cases in Florida keep climbing about a month after three counties declared states of emergency over the mosquito-borne illness.

item.title: AI chatbots may worsen symptoms in people with psychosis
item.description: Conversational AI chatbots are a relatively new technology, but they are now ubiquitous, embedded in everything from customer service platforms to personal productivity tools. Such is their rapid adoption that potential negative consequences are yet to be fully understood.

item.title: AI chatbots can be a valuable health resource for older adults—if they embrace 'informed skepticism'
item.description: It's easy to stereotype older adults as tech-averse or novice tech users. Yet a growing number of adults age 60 and older are embracing artificial intelligence, using it for entertainment, planning trips and even accessing health information.

item.title: Weakened chromosome anchors may help explain age-related declines in egg quality
item.description: As many as one in six adults face fertility difficulties worldwide, research has shown, and the challenge becomes harder as they age. Starting around age 35, the risk of eggs carrying an abnormal number of chromosomes rises steeply, contributing to declining fertility and increasing miscarriage rates. Understanding why these errors occur is essential for improving reproductive outcomes.

item.title: Why do people still get polio in some countries and not in others?
item.description: On a busy street in Karachi, Pakistan, a health care worker kneels down so she's eye to eye with a toddler. She squeezes two drops of liquid onto the child's tongue. Then she takes out a purple marker and colors the child's pinkie fingernail so everyone can see that this toddler is now vaccinated against polio.

item.title: Adventurous play linked to better physical and mental health in children
item.description: The biggest international study ever on risky play has found that children who have more opportunities for outdoor adventurous play tend to have better physical and mental health, as well as improved social and cognitive development.

item.title: Exploring how autism reduces sensitivity to feedback on decisions
item.description: Some people who have autism spectrum disorder struggle to adapt to changing demands in their environment. In a new study in JNeurosci, researchers discovered this struggle may be because these individuals are less sensitive to feedback about their behavior than individuals who do not have autism. This work was led by Nathaniel Zuk at Nottingham Trent University and Jaroslav Slobodskoy-Plusnin at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in collaboration with colleagues at University College London and Hebrew University.

item.title: Chest 'digital twin' predicts light paths to help plan personalized pneumonia treatment
item.description: Researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) in Brazil and their international collaborators have created a computational model that can generate a "digital twin" of the human thorax. The goal is to personalize the treatment of respiratory diseases using a special type of light.

item.title: If Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts can get dangerous blood clots, so can you
item.description: Jalen Hurts is 28, a Super Bowl MVP and an elite athlete in peak physical condition. He was also recently diagnosed with blood clots in his leg and both lungs.

item.title: Detailed brain map reveals how the insula shapes bodily sensations and processes pain
item.description: Tucked deep within the human brain's lateral fissure, beneath layers of the cerebral cortex, lies the insula. It is the hub that controls sensations ranging from pain and physical touch to hunger and emotions. Yet, it remains an enigma that neuroscientists have been trying to crack for ages. A recent study published in Nature has presented a new, detailed picture of certain regions of the insula that not only provides a new perspective but also questions some older ones.

item.title: Metabolic vulnerability identified in small cell lung cancer
item.description: Researchers at the University of Cologne have demonstrated that, while various cellular states of small cell lung cancer are equally dependent on the amino acid cysteine, they react differently when deprived of it. While some cancer cells subsequently die via ferroptosis—a form of cell death in which harmful oxidized fats accumulate in the cell membranes—others undergo apoptosis, a controlled, programmed form of cell death.

item.title: Wireless neural chip tracks brain changes in real time after Alzheimer's drug administration
item.description: A joint research team led by KAIST has used a small, implantable neural chip to wirelessly monitor real-time changes in a neurotransmitter involved in memory and learning after an Alzheimer's drug has been administered. In miniature pigs (minipigs), the team observed an increase in the neurotransmitter signal following drug administration, followed by a gradual return to baseline. The technology could help researchers assess how drugs act in the brain and develop stimulation methods that adapt to the brain's response.

item.title: Reproductive health and cystic fibrosis: New guidance offers options and hope
item.description: For much of the history of cystic fibrosis (CF) care, reproductive health was not a major part of the conversation. Fertility challenges were the norm for men and women with this genetic disorder, and many grew up assuming biological parenthood was not possible.

item.title: Black patients can face longer breast cancer care delays, study finds
item.description: Black patients and people with a learning disability face longer waiting times at key stages of breast cancer care, according to a nationwide study led by the University of Surrey.

item.title: AI-based computer model offers new weapon against hard-to-treat cancers
item.description: In a new paper published in Cell Reports Medicine, the UCL team outlines how they, in collaboration with a University of Cambridge team, developed a new type of treatment-predicting computer program that uses an individual's detailed genetic fingerprint to explore which treatments, if any, may kill their cancer—especially when standard treatments have failed.

item.title: AI could help identify people at higher risk of common cancers using routine health data
item.description: Machine learning models using routinely collected health information, such as blood tests, medical history and lifestyle factors, could help identify people at higher risk of several common cancers, according to an international study reported at the ESMO Congress 2026.
